# Dasakanipāta (AN 10)

**ID:** AN 10  
**Section:** Aṅguttaranikāya (an)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Dasakanipāta

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dasakanipāta* ("The Book of the Tens") constitutes the tenth major section (*nipāta*) of the *Aṅguttaranikāya*. Conforming to the numerical taxonomy of the collection, its suttas are arranged around doctrines, qualities, and practices organized into sets of ten [Norman 1983]. Kenneth Roy Norman notes that in the higher-numbered *nipātas*, combinations of smaller numbers are sometimes utilized to assemble the required total, and that the rigid division into chapters (*vaggas*) of ten occasionally severed doctrinally interconnected discourses [Norman 1983]. Norman also observes that the closing suttas enumerate ten qualities needed to destroy lust, which directly parallel the eleven qualities listed in the succeeding *Ekādasakanipāta* [Norman 1983]. The text was edited for the Pali Text Society by Edmund Hardy [Bendall 1893].

Several discourses in the *Dasakanipāta* receive targeted scholarly analysis. In the *Kāḷīsutta* (AN 10.26), the elder Mahākaccāna displays his exegetical skill by transposing a verse from "The Maiden's Questions" (SN 4.25) into systematic doctrine for the laywoman Kāḷī, while in AN 10.172 monks seek his detailed exposition of a terse summary statement delivered by the Buddha [Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003]. In the *Girimānandasutta* (AN 10.60), the Buddha instructs Ānanda on ten meditative perceptions—ranging from impermanence and anatomical parts to mindfulness of breathing—to alleviate the illness of the venerable Girimānanda [Anālayo 2016]. Later in the collection, the *Karajakāya-sutta* (AN 10.208) and the *Sañcetanika-sutta* (AN 10.206) examine intentional karma (*sañcetanika-kamma*) and the liberative mental development of the immeasurables, particularly benevolence (*mettācetovimutti*) [Martini 2012].

Suttas of the *Dasakanipāta* exhibit widespread parallels in non-Pali canonical collections, notably the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (28 suttas), *Madhyama-āgama* (18 suttas), and *Ekottarikāgama* (11 suttas), as well as individual texts like the Tibetan *Giriyānanda-sūtra* (D 38, parallel to AN 10.60) and MĀ 15 / Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośopāyikā* quotations parallel to AN 10.206 and AN 10.208 [Anālayo 2016; Martini 2012].
